title: Loops that wait for a condition

questions.q: Press Run and watch the numbers come down.

teach.say: A while loop repeats for as long as its condition stays true. It has three parts. Set the variable before the loop. Test it in the condition. Change it inside the loop. Miss out that last part and the condition never becomes false, so the loop never stops.

brief: Nothing is marked on this one.
A while loop that never changes its variable runs for ever.
The site stops a runaway program after a few seconds. It is a normal mistake, not a disaster.
questions.starter:
n = 3
while n > 0:
    print(n)
    n = n - 1
print("Lift off")
lines: Set n to 3 before the loop starts.
Keep going while n is above 0.
Show what n is holding.
Take 1 off n, so the condition gets closer to false.
This line is not indented, so it runs once, after the loop.
questions.fb: Three parts: n is set before the loop, tested in the condition, and made smaller inside it.

questions.q: What will this program display?
brief: Read every line before you choose.

teach.say: A while loop can count upwards as well. The condition is tested before every turn, so the loop stops as soon as the condition is false.

questions.fb: n reaches 4, the condition 4 < 4 is false, and the loop stops before 4 is ever displayed.

questions.q: Change the program so it displays the numbers 1 to 6, one on each line.
brief: Change only the number in the condition.
Display the numbers 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6, one on each line.

hint.think: The condition decides how far the loop goes before it stops.

questions.starter:
n = 1
while n <= 3:
    print(n)
    n = n + 1

tests.why: The loop still stops at 3, so the number in the condition was not changed.

questions.fb: The condition is where a while loop's finishing point lives.

questions.q: Finish the program so it counts down from the number typed in to 1, one number on each line.

teach.say: The line that changes the variable goes inside the loop, indented like the print. Without it the condition is tested on the same value every turn.

brief: The first three lines are written for you.
The user types in one whole number, which is never less than 1.
Replace ____ with one instruction of your own.
Display the numbers from the one typed down to 1, one on each line.

hint.think: The number has to get smaller on every turn, or the condition stays true for ever.
walk: The loop runs while n is above 0.
Something inside the loop has to bring n closer to 0.

questions.starter:
n = int(input())
while n > 0:
    print(n)
    ____

tests.why: Replace the ____ with an instruction that makes n smaller.
A 1 gives exactly one turn, because 0 is not above 0.
If this never finished, n was never changed inside the loop.

questions.fb: Set it, test it, change it. The third part is the one beginners leave out.

questions.q: Ask the user for a whole number. Using a while loop, display every number from 1 up to that number, one on each line.

teach.say: A counting while loop sets its counter before the loop, tests it against the finishing value, and adds 1 to it inside the loop.

lines: The finishing value, written into the program here.
Set the counter before the loop.
Keep going while the counter has not passed the finishing value.
Show the counter.
Add 1 to the counter, so the loop gets closer to stopping.
brief: The user types in one whole number, which is never less than 1.
The number typed in is displayed as well, on the last line.
Use a while loop, not a for loop.

hint.think: You need a counter of your own, because a while loop does not make one for you.

questions.starter: # Count up to the number typed in
require: This one is for practising the while loop, so your program has to use one.

tests.why: Nothing came out, so the counter was never displayed inside the loop.
A 1 gives one line. Nothing at all means the condition used < where <= was needed.
If this never finished, the counter was not changed inside the loop.

questions.fb: A while loop will count for you, but you have to set the counter up and move it on yourself.

questions.q: Ask the user for a whole number. Using a while loop, display every even number from 2 up to that number, one on each line.
brief: The user types in one whole number, which is never less than 2.
Start at 2 and go up in twos.
Display the number typed in as well, if it is even.

hint.think: The counter does not have to go up by 1. What would make it skip the odd numbers?

questions.starter: # Even numbers, 2 upwards

tests.why: 7 is odd, so the last line is 6. The counter steps by 2, not by 1.
A 2 gives one line. Nothing at all means the condition stopped before the first turn.
10 is even, so it is displayed too. Use <= and not < in the condition.

questions.fb: The size of the step is yours to choose, and it is what decides which numbers the loop lands on.

questions.q: This program should display 5, 4, 3, 2, 1, one on each line. It never stops. Find the mistake and put it right.

teach.say: A while loop tests the same variable over and over. If nothing inside the loop changes that variable, the condition stays true and the loop runs for ever. The site stops a runaway program after a few seconds. Every programmer writes one sooner or later.

brief: Press Run first and watch what happens.
Do not change the number 5 or the condition.
Display 5, 4, 3, 2 and 1, one on each line.

hint.think: Which of the three parts of a while loop is missing here?
walk: n is set to 5 before the loop.
n is tested in the condition.
Nothing inside the loop ever changes n.

tests.why: The loop never stopped, because n stayed at 5 for ever. Add a line inside the loop that makes n smaller.

questions.fb: A loop that runs for ever is the commonest while loop mistake there is, and the cure is always the same: change the variable inside the loop.

questions.q: Ask the user for a whole number. Using a while loop, display the line Step [number] for every number from 1 up to that number.
brief: The user types in one whole number, which is never less than 1.
There is one space after the word Step.
One line of output for each number.

hint.think: A number has to be turned into text before it can be joined to a word.

questions.starter: # Step 1, Step 2, and so on

tests.why: Join the word Step to the counter with str( ) round the counter.
One number gives one line.
The counter changes every turn, so each line is different.

questions.fb: str() round a number is how it joins onto words, and that has not changed now the number comes from a loop.

questions.q: Ask the user for a whole number. Using a while loop, display every number from it down to 1, one on each line. Then, using a second while loop, display every number from 1 back up to it, one on each line.
brief: The user types in one whole number, which is never less than 1.
The numbers come down first, then go back up.
The number 1 appears twice, once at the end of the first loop and once at the start of the second.

hint.think: Two separate loops, one after the other, each with its own counter set up before it.
walk: Read the number.
Count down to 1 in the first loop.
Set a counter back to 1.
Count up to the number in the second loop.

questions.starter: # Down to 1, then back up again

tests.why: Six lines from a 3: three coming down and three going up.
A 1 gives one turn in each loop, so the line appears twice.
The second loop needs its counter set back to 1 before it starts.

questions.fb: Two loops in one program each keep their own count, and the second one has to be set up just as carefully as the first.

questions.q: Press Run. Type 0 and press Enter, then type 12 and press Enter.

teach.say: A while loop can keep asking until the answer is allowed. Read one value before the loop. Then, while the value is still wrong, say so and read another.

brief: Nothing is marked on this one.
The 0 is refused, so the program asks again.
A loop like this one is called validation.
questions.starter:
age = int(input("Age? "))
while age < 1:
    print("Too small")
    age = int(input("Age? "))
print("Thank you")
lines: Read the first value before the loop.
Keep going while the value is still not allowed.
Tell the user what is wrong.
Read another value, which the condition then tests.
This runs once, when the value is finally allowed.
questions.fb: Reading once before the loop is what lets a good first answer skip the loop altogether.

questions.q: The user types 3, then 7, then 15. What will this program display?
brief: Read every line before you choose.

teach.say: Every refused value gets its own line, because the warning is inside the loop. The accepted value is displayed after the loop.

questions.fb: Two numbers were refused, so there are two warnings, and only the accepted one is displayed.

questions.q: Change the program so it keeps asking until the number is 10 or more.
brief: Change only the number in the condition.
A number of exactly 10 is accepted.
Display too small for each number refused.

hint.think: The condition says what counts as wrong, so that is the part to change.

questions.starter:
n = int(input())
while n < 5:
    print("too small")
    n = int(input())
print(n)

tests.why: A 7 is still being accepted, so the condition still stops at 5.
Exactly 10 is allowed, so the condition uses < and not <=.
A good first number is accepted straight away and nothing is refused.

questions.fb: One number in the condition decides what the program will accept.

questions.q: Finish the program so it keeps asking until the mark typed in is 100 or less.

teach.say: The second reading goes at the bottom of the loop. Then the condition tests the new value before the loop decides whether to go round again.

brief: The user types in whole numbers, one on each line, until one of them is 100 or less.
Replace ____ with one instruction of your own.
Display too big for each mark refused.
Then display the accepted mark on a line of its own.

hint.think: Without a new value inside the loop, the condition tests the same wrong mark for ever.

questions.starter:
mark = int(input())
while mark > 100:
    print("too big")
    ____
print(mark)

tests.why: Replace the ____ with an instruction that reads another mark.
Exactly 100 is allowed, so nothing is refused.
Two marks refused gives two warnings, so the reading must happen on every turn.

questions.fb: A validation loop reads twice: once before the loop, and once at the bottom of the body.

questions.q: Keep asking the user for a whole number until one of them is 1 or more. Display Too small for every number refused. Then display the accepted number on a line of its own.

teach.say: The condition describes what is wrong, not what is right. Here anything below 1 is wrong, so the loop keeps going while the value is below 1.

brief: The user types in whole numbers, one on each line, until one of them is 1 or more.
A number of exactly 1 is accepted.
Display exactly: Too small

hint.think: Read one number before the loop, then keep reading while the number is still wrong.

questions.starter: # Keep asking until the number reaches 1

tests.why: One number refused gives one warning, then the accepted number.
A good first number is accepted, so the loop runs zero times.
Two numbers refused gives two warnings. One only means an if was used where a while was needed.

questions.fb: An if asks once and gives up. A while keeps asking, which is exactly what validation needs.

questions.q: Keep asking the user for a whole number until one of them is from 1 to 5. Display Out of range for every number refused. Then display the accepted number on a line of its own.

teach.say: There are two ways of being wrong here, too small and too big, so the two comparisons are joined with or. Either one of them means asking again.

brief: The user types in whole numbers, one on each line, until one of them is from 1 to 5.
Both 1 and 5 are accepted.
Display exactly: Out of range

hint.think: Two ways of being wrong, joined so that either one keeps the loop going.

questions.starter: # Keep asking until the number is from 1 to 5

tests.why: One number below the range and one above it, so both halves of the condition are needed.
1 is the bottom of the range and is allowed, so the condition uses < 1 and not <= 1.
5 is the top of the range and is allowed, so the condition uses > 5 and not >= 5.
6 is just outside the range, which is where < and <= get mixed up.

questions.fb: Join the two ways of being wrong with or, and the loop keeps going while either of them is still true.

questions.q: This program should keep asking until the number is 10 or more. It gives up after one go. Find the mistake and put it right.
brief: Press Run first and type 3, then 5, then 12.
Display too small for each number refused.
Then display the accepted number on a line of its own.

hint.think: An if checks once and then moves on. What checks again and again?

questions.starter:
n = int(input())
if n < 10:
    print("too small")
    n = int(input())
print(n)

tests.why: A 5 came out, so the program accepted the second wrong number instead of asking again.
A good first number is accepted either way, so this test passes already.
One number refused looks the same with an if, which is why one test is never enough.

questions.fb: An if and a while look alike and behave very differently: only one of them goes back and checks again.

questions.q: Keep asking the user for a word until it is yes or no. Display Please type yes or no for every other word. Then display the accepted word on a line of its own.

teach.say: Two answers are allowed, so the loop keeps going while the word is neither of them. That needs and: not the first one and not the second one.
code: c = input()   # the user types pink

brief: The user types in words, one on each line, until one of them is yes or no.
The words are compared exactly, so y is not the word yes.
Display exactly: Please type yes or no

hint.think: The word is wrong when it is not the first answer and also not the second.

questions.starter: # Keep asking until the answer is yes or no

tests.why: One word refused gives one warning, then the accepted word.
Both yes and no are accepted. A warning here means the condition only tests for one of them.
Two words refused gives two warnings.
y is not the word yes, so it is refused. Comparing one letter would let it through.

questions.fb: Use and to rule out both allowed answers. With or the condition is always true, and the loop would never stop.

questions.q: Keep asking the user for a whole number until one of them is 10 or more. Display Too small for every number refused. Then keep asking for a word until it is yes or no. Display Please type yes or no for every word refused. Then display the accepted number. Then display the accepted word on the next line.
brief: The user types in whole numbers first, then words.
Two separate loops, one after the other.
The number is displayed before the word.
Display exactly: Too small, and exactly: Please type yes or no

hint.think: Two validations in one program, each with its own reading before its own loop.
walk: Read a number and keep asking while it is too small.
Read a word and keep asking while it is neither answer.
Display the number, then the word.

questions.starter: # A number to validate, then a word

tests.why: One number refused and one word refused, then the two accepted values.
Both first answers are allowed, so neither loop runs at all.
The number loop must finish before the word loop starts reading.

questions.fb: Each value gets its own validation loop, and the second loop does not begin until the first has an answer it accepts.

questions.q: Press Run. Type red, then blue, then stop.

teach.say: A sentinel is a value that means finish rather than real data. Read one value before the loop. Use it inside the loop. Read the next one at the bottom of the loop, so the condition tests it before it is ever used.

brief: Nothing is marked on this one.
The word stop is the signal to finish, so it is not displayed.
A value that means stop is called a sentinel.
questions.starter:
word = input("Word? ")
while word != "stop":
    print(word)
    word = input("Word? ")
print("Finished")
lines: Read the first word before the loop.
Keep going while the word is not the sentinel.
Use the word, because the condition has already let it through.
Read the next word, which the condition then tests.
This runs once, after the sentinel has been typed.
questions.fb: The sentinel is never used, because the condition tests every value before the body gets to it.

questions.q: The user types 5, then 8, then 0. What will this program display?
brief: Read every line before you choose.

teach.say: The sentinel is read like any other value, but the condition sends the loop home before the body can display it.

questions.fb: The 0 is the signal to stop, so it never reaches the print inside the loop.

questions.q: Change the program so the word end stops the loop instead of the word stop.
brief: Change only the sentinel in the condition.
Display each word as it is typed, one on each line.
Do not display the word end.

hint.think: The sentinel lives in the condition, inside quotation marks.

questions.starter:
word = input()
while word != "stop":
    print(word)
    word = input()

tests.why: The word end came out or the program crashed, so end is not yet the sentinel.
One word before the sentinel gives one line.
Every word before end is displayed, however many there are.

questions.fb: Changing the sentinel changes nothing else: the shape of the loop stays exactly the same.

questions.q: Finish the program so it displays each number until -1 is typed.

teach.say: The reading at the bottom of the loop is what lets the next value be tested before it is used. Leave it out and the first value is tested for ever.

brief: The user types in whole numbers, one on each line, until they type -1.
Replace ____ with one instruction of your own.
Display each number as it is typed, one on each line.
Do not display the -1.

hint.think: The loop needs the next number before it tests the condition again.

questions.starter:
n = int(input())
while n != -1:
    print(n)
    ____

tests.why: Replace the ____ with an instruction that reads the next number.
One number before the sentinel gives one line.
A 0 is ordinary data here and is displayed, because only -1 stops the loop.

questions.fb: Read one before the loop, read the next at the bottom. That pair is the whole pattern.

questions.q: Ask the user for whole numbers until they type 0, which means stop. Display each number doubled, one on each line. Do not display anything for the 0.
brief: The user types in whole numbers, one on each line, until they type 0.
At least one number comes before the 0.
One line of output for each number, which is that number multiplied by 2.

hint.think: The doubling happens inside the loop, to the value the condition has let through.

questions.starter: # Double each number until 0 stops the loop

tests.why: Two numbers before the 0 gives two lines, each one doubled.
One number gives one line.
Negative numbers are ordinary data, because only 0 stops the loop.

questions.fb: The sentinel loop reads, tests, then uses. Nothing is done to a value until the condition has allowed it.

questions.q: Ask the user for whole numbers until they type -1, which means stop. Add the numbers up. Display the total and nothing else.

teach.say: A running total works the same here as it did in a for loop. Set it to 0 before the loop, add to it inside the loop, and display it after the loop.

brief: The user types in whole numbers, one on each line, until they type -1.
The -1 is not added to the total.
With no numbers at all the total is 0, and that 0 is still displayed.

hint.think: Three places for the total: set before, added inside, displayed after.

questions.starter: # Add the numbers up until -1 stops the loop

tests.why: The three numbers come to 60. A 59 means the -1 was added as well.
No numbers at all, so the total is still 0, and it still has to be displayed.
One number only. Check the total starts at 0 rather than at the first number.
However many numbers there are, the same loop handles them.

questions.fb: Set it, add to it, display it. A while loop handles a running total exactly as a for loop does.

questions.q: This program should add up the numbers typed before the -1. It adds the -1 as well. Find the mistake and put it right.

teach.say: The order of the two lines inside the loop decides which values get used. Read at the bottom of the loop, so the condition tests every value before the body touches it.

brief: Press Run first and type 10, then 20, then -1.
The -1 is the signal to stop and is not part of the total.
Display the total and nothing else.
With no numbers at all the total is 0.

hint.think: Which values reach the line that adds to the total?
walk: Read one number before the loop.
Add it inside the loop.
Read the next number at the bottom of the loop.

questions.starter:
total = 0
n = 0
while n != -1:
    n = int(input())
    total = total + n
print(total)

tests.why: A 29 means the -1 was added. Move the reading to the bottom of the loop.
No numbers at all, so the total is 0. A -1 here means the sentinel was treated as data.
One number only, and the -1 must not change the total.

questions.fb: Reading at the top of the loop lets the sentinel into the body. Reading at the bottom keeps it out.

questions.q: Ask the user for whole numbers until they type the word end, which means stop. Add the numbers up. Display the line Total is [total].

teach.say: When the sentinel is a word, the line has to be read as text. It is turned into a number inside the loop, once the condition has shown it is not the sentinel.

brief: The user types in whole numbers, one on each line, then the word end to finish.
Read each line as text, and cast it to a number inside the loop.
With no numbers at all the total is 0.
There is one space after the word is.

hint.think: int() on the word end would crash, so the line must stay text until the condition has let it through.

questions.starter: # Numbers as text, cast inside the loop

tests.why: The two numbers come to 20, and each line is cast with int( ) before it is added.
The loop runs zero times. A crash means int( ) was used on the word end.
One number only, and the message still has to be displayed.
int( ) copes with a minus sign, but the line is still read as text first.

questions.fb: Read as text, test the condition, then cast. Casting too early is what makes a word sentinel crash.

questions.q: Ask the user for whole numbers until they type -1, which means stop. Display each number as it is typed, one on each line. Then display the line Highest was [the largest number]. Display none instead when -1 is the very first number typed.
brief: The user types in whole numbers, one on each line, until they type -1.
The numbers may be negative.
Display exactly: none
There is one space after the word was.

hint.think: A largest so far that starts at 0 can never be beaten by a negative number.
walk: Read the first number.
If it is the sentinel, display none.
Otherwise make it the largest so far, then loop, displaying and comparing.
Then display the Highest was line.

questions.starter: # Show each number, then the largest of them

tests.why: Three numbers, then the largest. A 2 at the end means the last number was displayed rather than the largest.
Nothing was typed, so there is no largest to report.
With one number, that number is the largest.
Both numbers are below 0, so a largest starting at 0 would never be beaten.

questions.fb: A largest so far starts at the first value read, never at 0, because the data is allowed to be negative.

questions.q: Press Run. Type red, then blue, then end.

teach.say: A counter is a total that always goes up by 1. Set it to 0 before the loop, add 1 to it inside the loop, and display it after the loop.

brief: Nothing is marked on this one.
The word end is the sentinel, so it is not counted.
The count is displayed once, after the loop.
questions.starter:
count = 0
word = input("Word? ")
while word != "end":
    count = count + 1
    word = input("Word? ")
print(count)
lines: Set the counter to 0 before the loop.
Read the first word.
Keep going while the word is not the sentinel.
Add 1 to the counter for this word.
Read the next word.
Display the counter once the loop has finished.
questions.fb: The counter counts turns of the loop, so it does not matter what the values themselves are.

questions.q: What will this program display?
brief: Read every line before you choose.
Work out what n is at the start of each turn.

teach.say: The counter and the variable in the condition are two different things. One counts the turns and the other decides when to stop.

questions.fb: n goes 1, 3, 5. The loop runs twice, because 5 is not below 5, so the counter reaches 2.

questions.q: Change the program so it displays tick ten times instead of five times.
brief: Change only the number in the condition.
Display exactly: tick
Ten lines of output.

hint.think: The counter here is also the variable the condition tests.

questions.starter:
count = 0
while count < 5:
    print("tick")
    count = count + 1

tests.why: There are still five lines, so the number in the condition was not changed.

questions.fb: One counter can do two jobs at once: count the turns and decide when to stop.

questions.q: Finish the program so it displays how many words were typed before the word end.
brief: The user types in words, one on each line, then the word end to finish.
Replace ____ with one instruction of your own.
The word end is not counted.
Display one number and nothing else.

hint.think: The counter is already set to 0. It just never goes up.

questions.starter:
count = 0
word = input()
while word != "end":
    ____
    word = input()
print(count)

tests.why: Replace the ____ with an instruction that adds 1 to the counter.
No words at all, so the count is 0, and that 0 is still displayed.
One word gives a count of 1.

questions.fb: A counter that is never added to stays at 0, however many times the loop goes round.

questions.q: Ask the user for whole numbers until they type -1, which means stop. Count how many numbers were typed. Display the count and nothing else.
brief: The user types in whole numbers, one on each line, until they type -1.
The -1 is not counted.
With no numbers at all the count is 0, and that 0 is still displayed.

hint.think: The counter goes up once for every turn of the loop.

questions.starter: # Count the numbers until -1 stops the loop

tests.why: Three numbers were typed. A 4 means the -1 was counted as well.
Nothing was typed, so the count is 0.
One number gives a count of 1.
A 0 is a number like any other and still counts, because only -1 stops the loop.

questions.fb: The counter counts turns, so a 0 or a negative number counts just as much as a big one.

questions.q: Ask the user for whole numbers until they type -1, which means stop. Count how many of them are 50 or more. Display the count and nothing else.

teach.say: An if inside the loop decides which turns count. The counter then goes up on some turns and not on others.

brief: The user types in whole numbers, one on each line, until they type -1.
A number of exactly 50 counts.
Display one number and nothing else.

hint.think: Every number goes round the loop, but only some of them should move the counter.

questions.starter: # Count only the numbers that reach 50

tests.why: Two of the three numbers reach 50, and only the count is displayed.
No numbers at all, so the count is 0. The counter has to be set before the loop.
49 does not reach 50, so nothing is counted.
Exactly 50 counts, so all three do. A 1 here means > 50 was used instead of >= 50.

questions.fb: The loop visits every value and the if decides which ones are worth counting.

questions.q: This program should display how many numbers were typed before the -1. It always displays 1. Find the mistake and put it right.
brief: Press Run first and type 4, then 7, then 9, then -1.
The -1 is not counted.
Display one number and nothing else.

hint.think: A counter is set up once. What happens if it is set to 0 again on every turn?
walk: Look at the two lines inside the loop that touch count.
One of them belongs above the loop, not inside it.

questions.starter:
n = int(input())
while n != -1:
    count = 0
    count = count + 1
    n = int(input())
print(count)

tests.why: The counter was wiped back to 0 at the start of every turn, so it never got past 1.
One number gives 1 either way, which is why one test is never enough.
Set the counter to 0 once, before the loop.

questions.fb: Setting a counter up belongs before the loop. Inside the loop it wipes out everything counted so far.

questions.q: Ask the user for whole numbers until they type -1, which means stop. Count how many numbers were typed. Add them up. Display the count. Then display the total on the next line.
brief: The user types in whole numbers, one on each line, until they type -1.
The -1 is neither counted nor added.
Two lines of output: the count first, then the total.
With no numbers at all both lines display 0.

hint.think: Two things to keep track of, so two variables set up before the loop.

questions.starter: # Count them and add them up at the same time

tests.why: Three numbers coming to 60, so the two lines are different.
No numbers at all, so both counters are still 0 and both lines are displayed.
With one number the count is 1 and the total is that number.
Two numbers that cancel out, so the count and the total differ.

questions.fb: One pass through the data can keep as many running values as you like, as long as each has its own variable.

questions.q: Ask the user for whole numbers until they type -1, which means stop. Count how many of them are above 0. Count how many are below 0. Display the line [how many] above zero. Then display the line [how many] below zero on the next line.
brief: The user types in whole numbers, one on each line, until they type -1.
A 0 is neither above nor below, so it is not counted at all.
Two lines of output, the above line first.
There is one space after each number.

hint.think: Two counters and an if with an elif, because a number cannot be in both groups.

questions.starter: # Count the numbers above zero and below zero

count = 0
for i in range(5):
    n = n // 2
    count = count + 1
print(count)

tests.why: 8 halves to 4, then 2, then 1, which is three turns, not five.
